extracted.intended_audience: mathematics faculty, calculus instructors, department leaders, and curriculum/evaluation researchers involved in undergraduate calculus reform
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for designing, implementing, and evaluating undergraduate calculus reform courses and their assessment practices, including classroom structures, grading policies, data-collection methods, and departmental considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACE teaching cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACE teaching cycle: a weekly repetition of (A) activities in a computer lab, (C) classroom discussion based on those activities, and (E) exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer activities are intended to directly foster specific mental constructions; classroom discussions get students to reflect on these constructions and use them to develop understandings of mathematical concepts; exercises (fairly traditional) reinforce and extend developing mathematical knowledge. (Original phrasing: "The computer activities are intended to directly foster the specific mental constructions...; the classroom discussions are intended to get students to reflect...; and the exercises... are expected to help the students reinforce and extend their developing mathematical knowledge.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of participation/completion as proxy for mental constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the pedagogy operated as intended — the student participated in all course activities, cooperated in her or his group, completed the assignments, did reasonably well in exams — then research-based assertions may be applied that the mental constructions were made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because in-depth interviews and analyses are impractical, the instructor should record written work, classroom participation, and group meetings and use successful performance on designed computer tasks and related tests as indirect evidence that students have constructed the target understandings (e.g., understanding of the chain rule as composition/process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment focus on depth (hardest questions) rather than breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: When making up an examination, prioritize asking the hardest possible questions about the material believed to have been learned rather than trying to cover as large a portion of material as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how hard the tests were and how much material they covered as part of assessing course effectiveness. The assumption is that students who score x on a limited test understand x amount of tested material (and, by assumption, x of untested material) — accept limits of examination sampling and consider test difficulty in course evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grade composition and weighting policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Final grades are determined by a combination of course components (six scores: four group scores and two individual), with most components given equal weight and classroom participation used to resolve borderline cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment items: weekly computer assignments (group submission), weekly exercises (group submission), first exam (group exam, every student receives same grade), second exam (individual; each student receives individual score and the group's average), final exam (individual, standard time period), classroom participation (recorded; used to resolve borderline). If individual scores differ sharply from group scores, adjust final grade by as much as a single letter toward the individual scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly computer assignments grading philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly computer assignments are graded relatively leniently and are intended to stimulate mental constructions, often measuring mental effort as much as correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students work on them in groups during lab time but must finish substantial work outside lab (individually or in collaboration). Submissions are by group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam administration and format as assessment design
rubrics_metrics.description: First and second exams may be administered without time limits (held throughout an entire day) with honor-system flexibility to leave and return; first exam can be a group exam, second exam individual with group-average consideration, final exam standard timed individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide conditions (e.g., full-day exams, group vs individual formats) that align with intended learning outcomes. Make clear grading consequences (group grades shared, second exam yields two grades: personal and group average).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative learning reward structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For cooperative learning to be more likely beneficial, students should be rewarded individually for the performance of their group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement reward/assessment mechanisms that provide individual accountability tied to group success (citing Slavin). Consider using group work combined with individual measures to maintain individual incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of assessment data for decision making
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment data should be used to assign grades, to reconsider specific parts of the course, and to reconsider the entire pedagogical approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine course-specific information about each student with general research findings to make formative decisions; on borderline grades, favor the higher grade when course components indicate the course 'went well' in intended terms and students bought into the approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation rules for interpreting mismatches between assessment and research
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessment results and research-based expectations disagree, follow a structured interpretation: (a) research predicts understanding but students do not perform → examine implementation for that concept; (b) students perform well but research suggests poor understanding → suspect memorization or superficial strategies; (c) both course performance and research suggest students are 'not getting it' → consider local revisions to approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this triangulation as a formative diagnostic to guide targeted revisions to activities, discussion prompts, or materials for specific concepts (example: revise approach to limits when tasks and exams show poor performance and research offers no evidence of improved understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation criterion for systemic program change
rubrics_metrics.description: If, over time, student performance in courses and research indicates persistent failure of the approach, consider more systemic changes, including the possibility of rejecting the entire approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track longitudinal patterns; only after repeated or sustained evidence of poor outcomes should large-scale program termination be considered. So far, authors note this has not happened in their projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental environment and commitment as success factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of reform is heavily dependent on the educational environment created: departmental commitment and amount of faculty involvement are critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs supported by only a small portion of faculty face inconsistency and exhaustion of reformers; anticipate problems, plan methods to handle them, and provide resources such as technical and educational faculty support, special study sessions, and computer assistance for students. Strive for departmental-level consistency and broad faculty buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of questionnaires to initiate departmental dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Use targeted questionnaires (e.g., items from the CCH EDP survey) to prompt department discussions about goals, expectations, technology use, pedagogical methods, and definitions of rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questionnaire items can be used anonymously before meetings, modified for local contexts, collated and analyzed, and serve as foundations for formal discussions. Example discussion prompts provided: characterize your department’s approach to calculus; is technology the basis for efforts; do efforts encourage student engagement and how do you know; what role do cooperative groups/projects/presentations/concrete materials play; what does 'rigor' mean and how important is it?

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation-methodological standards for studying reform
rubrics_metrics.description: A thorough evaluation should combine multiple data-collection methods: literature search, review of project documentation (e.g., NSF folders), mailed/email surveys to participants, and development of a qualitative database with a predefined framework and precise definitions to guide data entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the evaluation framework in consultation with program officers, define precise coding/definitions for presence of evaluation/dissemination/reform activities, and cross-analyze between projects; use triangulation of sources for preliminary and final reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research priorities for future evaluation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Further studies should employ more in-depth, rigorous data collection, including long-term impact studies and investigations of the impact of reform on faculty, departments, and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should not only examine how students learn, but the actual impact of different educational environments created by reform; studies should also explore methods for developing teaching styles of current and future instructors to support reform implementation and inform resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting mixed outcome measures
rubrics_metrics.description: When different assessment measures yield mixed results (e.g., better conceptual understanding and retention but mixed scores on traditional exams), interpret such outcomes cautiously and examine both types of measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that reform students may show higher conceptual understanding, retention, and confidence yet not uniformly outperform on traditional skill-based exams; use a mix of conceptual and traditional measures when evaluating trade-offs and making policy/resource decisions.
